strengths: Novel and timely extension of the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) from unimodal LLMs to a vision-language model (OpenFlamingo-4B), addressing a genuine gap since prior multimodal task-vector work (Hojel et al. 2024; Huang et al. 2024) has not targeted relational/spatial reasoning specifically.

The methodology is methodologically consistent with established causal mediation analysis (AIE) techniques, and the paper provides thorough ablations on injection layer, head-set size, and context size, which strengthen the mechanistic claims that a sparse subset of intermediate-layer attention heads carries relational information.
Experiments span both a controlled synthetic dataset (enabling precise causal analysis) and a more realistic dataset (GQA), which helps assess whether findings generalize beyond artificial stimuli.

The composite function vector experiment for one-shot analogy with untrained relations (e.g., above-left) is a genuinely interesting test of the linear representation hypothesis in a multimodal setting, and shows the approach outperforms few-shot ICL baselines even with more demonstrations.

Reasonable transparency: dataset construction is described in detail, a reproducibility statement promises code/data release, and limitations (single architecture, limited relation set) are honestly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The study relies entirely on a single, relatively small and dated backbone (OpenFlamingo-4B, a 3B-language-model-based VLM); it is unclear whether the localized, extractable-and-fine-tunable function vector structure generalizes to modern, more capable LMMs (e.g., LLaVA-family, Qwen-VL, InternVL), which substantially limits the significance of the central claims about how 'LMMs' encode relational knowledge.

Absolute accuracies remain quite low throughout (e.g., ~20-25% on synthetic relations and ~20-48% on GQA relations even after fine-tuning; ~16.8% on the analogy task), which, despite relative improvements over baselines, raises questions about the practical usefulness and robustness of the extracted vectors for real relational reasoning.

The real-image (GQA) dataset is very small (201 images total, 101 for training/extraction), and no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests accompany the many bar-chart comparisons in Figures 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, making it hard to assess whether reported differences are robust or due to noise/small-sample variance.

The comparison between fine-tuned function vectors (trained on up to 1000 zero-shot examples with a dedicated optimization procedure) and 4-shot ICL is somewhat asymmetric in terms of supervision signal used, which complicates the interpretation of 'fine-tuned FV significantly outperforms ICL baselines' as a fair apples-to-apples comparison.

No direct empirical comparison to existing multimodal task-vector methods (e.g., Multimodal Task Vectors, Visual Task Vectors) is provided, even though these are discussed as related work; this omission makes it difficult to situate the proposed approach's benefits relative to prior alternatives.

The scope of relations is narrow (four basic spatial relations plus four compositional variants), and hyperparameters such as injection layer (19 for synthetic, 8 for GQA) appear tuned per-dataset without a clear held-out validation protocol described, raising a mild risk of selection bias in reported results.

strengths: The paper presents a reasonably novel extension of the function-vector framework (originally developed for LLMs by Todd et al. 2024) to a vision-language model, applying causal mediation analysis to isolate a sparse subset of attention heads responsible for spatial-relation encoding in OpenFlamingo-4B.

The experimental design is comprehensive in scope: it includes both a controlled synthetic dataset and a real-image (GQA) dataset, systematic ablations over injection layer, head-set size, and context size, and a fine-tuning procedure that keeps the backbone frozen while updating only the function vector.

The composite function vector idea for one-shot analogy tasks (linearly combining relation-specific vectors weighted by source-analogy likelihoods) is a creative and reasonably well-motivated test of the linear representation hypothesis in a multimodal setting, and the method is clearly illustrated (Figure 3).

The paper is generally clearly written, with formal problem definitions, explicit equations for the CIE/AIE/fine-tuning objectives, and an honest limitations section acknowledging the restriction to a single lightweight architecture and small relation set.
weaknesses: Absolute performance is low across nearly all conditions: even the best 'fine-tuned FV' condition rarely exceeds ~25-48% accuracy (Fig. 5), and the composite FV analogy result only reaches 16.8% accuracy (Fig. 6). The paper repeatedly claims results are 'significant' or show 'substantial gains,' but these are relative improvements over a very weak baseline, and it is unclear whether such low absolute accuracies represent a practically meaningful or reliable relational capability.

No statistical testing (confidence intervals, error bars, multiple seeds, significance tests) is reported anywhere in the main results (Figures 5, 6, 9, 10, 11), despite the frequent use of language like 'significantly outperform.' Given the modest test-set sizes (e.g., 200 tasks per relation in GQA, single evaluation runs), it is hard to assess whether observed differences are robust or within noise.

The real-image (GQA) evaluation is built on a very small curated set (201 images total, only 101 for training/extraction and 100 for test), which raises concerns about the reliability and generalizability of conclusions drawn from this dataset, especially for a paper making claims about 'localized internal structures' and general relational reasoning in LMMs.

The study is confined to a single, relatively old and lightweight architecture (OpenFlamingo-4B, built on a 3B RedPajama backbone), which the authors themselves acknowledge as a major limitation. No experiments are conducted on more recent or larger LMMs (e.g., LLaVA, IDEFICS, Flamingo-9B/80B), leaving open whether the reported mechanisms are an artifact of this specific, comparatively weak model rather than a general property of multimodal transformers.

Directly relevant prior work (Multimodal Task Vectors, Huang et al. 2024; Visual Task Vectors, Hojel et al. 2024) is discussed in related work but never empirically compared against, despite substantial conceptual overlap with the proposed multimodal function vectors — this omission makes it difficult to judge the actual novelty/advantage of the proposed method relative to existing multimodal task-vector approaches.

The relation set investigated is narrow (4 basic spatial relations in synthetic data, 7 in GQA), and the 'novel relation' generalization test (above-left, above-right, etc.) is itself just compositions of the same 4 trained primitives, which somewhat limits how surprising or strong the generalization claim actually is.

No ablation with a random/control vector of matched norm is reported to rule out the possibility that any sufficiently large perturbation to hidden states (not necessarily the causally-derived function vector) could produce similar gains over the zero-shot baseline — this weakens the causal interpretation claims.

The fine-tuning procedure requires per-relation supervised training data even though it is described as improving 'zero-shot' performance; this framing may overstate the zero-shot nature of the approach, since a held-out labeled training set specific to each relation is required to fine-tune the vector.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of the function vector (FV) framework from language-only transformers to a genuinely multimodal setting, addressing an identified gap in the literature (prior multimodal task-vector work focused on visual prompting/naming rather than relational reasoning).

Methodologically sound causal mediation analysis: the paper clearly formalizes AIE computation with carefully constructed 'uninformative context' perturbations that control for relation-type bias across the four demonstrations, which is a thoughtful experimental control.

Uses two complementary datasets (a controlled synthetic dataset and a curated real-image GQA subset), which strengthens the internal validity of the causal claims and shows the phenomenon is not an artifact of a single stimulus type.

Comprehensive ablation studies (injection layer, number of heads, context size) that both support the main claims and provide useful mechanistic insight (e.g., sparse mid-layer subnetworks, non-monotonic head-count effects).

The composite function vector idea for solving analogy problems with untrained relations is a creative and non-trivial extension, directly testing the linear representation hypothesis in a multimodal setting and providing a genuine test of generalization beyond simple interpolation.
Reasonable transparency: reproducibility statement with code/data release, explicit LLM-usage disclosure, and an honest limitations section that does not hide the restricted scope of the study.
weaknesses: All experiments rely on a single, relatively small and outdated backbone (OpenFlamingo-4B). Given known differences in attention/fusion mechanisms across modern LMM architectures (e.g., LLaVA-style, Qwen-VL, cross-attention vs. prefix-fusion models), it is unclear how much of the observed localization generalizes beyond this specific model, limiting the significance of the claims about LMMs in general.

Absolute accuracies remain low across the board even after fine-tuning (roughly 20-45% on 4-7-way tasks, and only 16.8% on the one-shot analogy task), which tempers claims of 'significantly outperforming' baselines in a practically meaningful sense; the paper would benefit from reporting confidence intervals or significance tests for the accuracy gaps shown in Figures 5 and 6.

The real-image GQA dataset is very small (201 images total, 101/100 train/test split), which limits statistical power and the strength of conclusions drawn from the real-image experiments relative to the synthetic ones.

The fine-tuning comparison is somewhat asymmetric: fine-tuned FVs are optimized on task-specific training data (1000 synthetic / 101 real images) while the ICL baselines use only a handful of static demonstrations; while this is stated, the framing as 'significantly outperforming ICL baselines' could be tempered by noting that FVs have access to substantially more supervision.

The paper does not empirically compare against the most closely related prior work, Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV, Huang et al. 2024), despite discussing it in related work; a direct comparison would better contextualize how much added value the causal-mediation-based extraction and composite-vector generalization provide over existing multimodal task-vector approaches.

The scope is restricted to four/seven basic spatial relations; the claims about 'relational reasoning in LMMs' and 'model modularity' are broad, but the empirical evidence covers only spatial relations, not other relation types (e.g., agentic, functional, social) that would be needed to substantiate the broader framing used in the abstract and conclusion (the authors do acknowledge this limitation).

strengths: The paper extends the function-vector framework (originally developed for LLMs) to multimodal models in a technically careful way, providing a full pipeline: causal mediation analysis to locate relation-encoding attention heads, zero-shot vector injection, fine-tuning of vectors with frozen backbones, and composite vectors for one-shot analogy with novel relations.

Experiments span two architecturally different LMMs (OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL) and two dataset types (controlled synthetic images and realistic GQA images with both spatial and agentic relations), which strengthens the generality of the claims.

Thorough ablation studies (injection layer, number of heads, context size during extraction) give useful mechanistic insight and support the claim that a sparse subset of intermediate-layer heads carries relational information.

Additional experiments—object generalization, cross-dataset transfer (Synthetic→GQA), and RSA comparison between models—go beyond the core claims and add robustness/transparency to the analysis, including honestly reporting a case (negative RSA correlation) that complicates the story rather than hiding it.

The composite function vector experiment for solving one-shot analogies with untrained relations is a nice demonstration of compositionality, connecting to the linear representation hypothesis in an empirically testable way.
weaknesses: Absolute accuracies remain quite low in several settings (e.g., OpenFlamingo synthetic FFV around 20-25%, GQA spatial FFV around 25-45%), which tempers claims of the method's practical utility even though relative gains over baselines are large; the paper would benefit from more discussion of why performance is still far below plausible ceiling.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported for the main accuracy comparisons (Table 1, Figure 6, Figure 7), making it hard to assess whether reported gains are robust or could be inflated by evaluation noise, especially given only single training/test splits are used.

The method requires white-box access to internal hidden states/attention head activations, which limits applicability to widely-used closed-source LMMs; this constraint is not clearly discussed as a limitation.

Direct quantitative comparison to closely related prior work (e.g., Multimodal Task Vectors, Visual Task Vectors) is missing; the paper only discusses these methods qualitatively in related work rather than benchmarking against them on the same tasks.

The RSA finding that function vectors are structurally dissimilar (even anti-correlated) across the two models raises questions about whether the identified 'localized internal structure' reflects a universal computational motif or is largely idiosyncratic per model, and this tension is not deeply analyzed beyond a brief appendix note.

The set of evaluated relations remains fairly narrow (4 spatial in synthetic, 7 spatial + 5 agentic in GQA), and the object/relation generalization tests use relatively small held-out sets (10 objects, 4 novel relations), limiting the strength of generalization claims.

The one-shot analogy/composite vector method is described as overcoming the limits of standard ICL, but it still requires a source demonstration to infer mixture weights, so it is not truly demonstration-free; this dependency is acknowledged only briefly as a limitation.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and well-motivated question: whether the function-vector framework from interpretability research on LLMs can be extended to multimodal relational reasoning, an underexplored area.

The experimental pipeline is comprehensive in scope, covering causal mediation analysis (AIE), zero-shot intervention, fine-tuning of extracted vectors, and a creative composite-vector analogy task, with ablations on layer, head-set size, and context size.
Two architecturally different LMMs (OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL) and both synthetic and real (GQA) datasets are used, which is a reasonable attempt at generality.
The synthetic dataset design with controlled object placement is a sensible way to isolate relational understanding from object recognition confounds.
Figures (e.g., AIE heatmaps, Figures 6 and 7) are generally clear and support the narrative of sparse, causally relevant attention heads.
weaknesses: Central claim undermined by own appendix result: Appendix G reports negative RSA correlations between OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL function vectors (r = -0.38 and -0.29), and near-orthogonal/negative pairwise cosine similarities for Qwen3-VL relation vectors (Table 3). This directly contradicts the abstract/conclusion's claim that 'these models encode visual relational knowledge within localized internal structures' in a generalizable way across models — this contradiction is not discussed or reconciled in the main text.

Missing critical control baselines: the 'fine-tuned function vector' is essentially a learned steering vector optimized by gradient descent directly on the task; there is no ablation comparing against a randomly initialized vector trained the same way, or a simple mean-difference/contrastive activation-addition vector without AIE-based head selection. Without this, it is unclear whether the causal-mediation machinery contributes anything beyond what a generic trainable offset vector would achieve.

Absolute performance remains low and highly variable across settings (e.g., 4-shot ICL only 26.8%/31.6%/57.7% across datasets; some FFV results still under 30%), raising concerns about the practical significance and reliability of the relational task itself (ambiguous ground-truth labels, e.g., multiple objects could plausibly satisfy a spatial relation in GQA).

No reported variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results for any accuracy numbers (Tables 1, Figures 6, 7), making it impossible to assess whether reported gains are statistically meaningful versus noise, especially given dataset-level stochastic sampling.

The one-shot analogy/composite vector experiment has a somewhat circular evaluation: the mixture weights are derived using the same LMM and the same base function vectors being evaluated, and the comparison to ICL baselines (which lack access to the per-relation structure) may not be entirely fair or informative about generalization to genuinely novel relations.

The method is largely an incremental application of an existing technique (Todd et al. 2024 function vectors) to a new modality, with limited additional methodological innovation beyond adapting the recipe to multimodal prompts; conceptual novelty is modest.

Limited relation/task diversity (only basic spatial and a handful of agentic relations) and only 4B-scale models are tested, limiting confidence that findings scale to larger or more diverse multimodal models or richer relation types.
The transfer experiment in Appendix F (Synthetic→GQA) is only shown for OpenFlamingo, not Qwen3-VL, and is not integrated into the core generalization claims made in the main text.

Presentation issue: important disconfirming results (Appendix G) are relegated to an appendix without being discussed or reconciled with the paper's central claims in the conclusion, which affects the honesty/completeness of the limitations discussion.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) from unimodal LLMs to large multimodal models, addressing a clear gap in the literature on visual relational reasoning.

Thorough experimental design spanning two distinct LMM architectures (OpenFlamingo, Qwen3-VL) and three datasets (controlled synthetic images plus two real-image GQA subsets for spatial and agentic relations), which strengthens the generality of the core claims.

The paper goes beyond simple extraction and shows a coherent pipeline of increasingly sophisticated interventions: causal mediation analysis to locate heads, zero-shot vector injection, fine-tuning of the vector with frozen backbone, and compositional combination of vectors for one-shot analogy with untrained relations -- each building naturally on the last.

Extensive ablations (injection layer, number of heads, context size) and supplementary analyses (cross-dataset transfer of vectors, representational similarity analysis between models) provide a relatively complete picture of the method's behavior and robustness, which is good practice for an interpretability paper.

Generalization experiments to novel objects and novel relation compositions (one-shot analogy for above-left/above-right/etc.) are a nice test of whether the vectors capture abstract relational structure rather than superficial correlations.
weaknesses: Absolute accuracies remain low in many conditions (e.g., OpenFlamingo fine-tuned vectors reach only ~13-22% on several settings, GQA spatial accuracies are below 0.5 even after fine-tuning), which tempers claims about the practical significance of the approach, even though relative improvements over baselines are substantial.

The representational similarity analysis in Appendix G reports a *negative* correlation between the two models' relational geometries (r = -0.38 and -0.29), and the pairwise similarity structure is qualitatively very different (OpenFlamingo heads are near-collinear across relations while Qwen3-VL heads are much more differentiated). This finding is in tension with the paper's framing that LMMs generically encode 'localized internal structures' for relations, and deserves more discussion/interpretation rather than being relegated to an appendix with little comment.

No comparison against other published multimodal interpretability/control baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., Multimodal Task Vectors (Huang et al., 2024) or Visual Task Vectors (Hojel et al., 2024)), despite these being closely related prior approaches; the only baselines are vanilla zero/few-shot ICL.

No reported variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results for any of the accuracy numbers, making it hard to judge whether reported gains (especially smaller ones, e.g., a few percentage points) are robust or within noise.

The two chosen backbones (OpenFlamingo-4B, Qwen3-VL-4B) are relatively small/older models; it's unclear whether the localized function-vector phenomenon and the magnitude of gains would hold for larger, more capable contemporary LMMs, limiting the generalizability of the conclusions.

Dataset construction involves a number of fairly ad hoc filtering heuristics (e.g., object area 5-30%, 4-7 valid objects per image, removal of 'non-descriptive' object categories) that are not well justified and could introduce selection biases favoring easier relational instances.

The paper does not provide a working link to the code repository in the manuscript text (only a footnote placeholder), which, combined with the complexity of the causal mediation and fine-tuning pipeline, raises some reproducibility concerns absent the actual released artifact.
